en: The Sūtra on the Daughter Nāgadattā, translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī in the Amrapālī Grove, together with a great [assembly].
The assembly of bhikṣus numbered one thousand two hundred and fifty, together with a multitude of five hundred bodhisattvas.
At dawn, the Buddha donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city for alms, followed by the entire assembly;
the devas, nāgas, and spirits offered incense, flowers, and music in double the usual measure.
The Buddha arrived at the gate of the householder Subhūti’s residence.
Subhūti had a daughter named Nāgadattā, who was fourteen years old; at that time, she was in the bathhouse bathing, anointing herself with fragrant unguents, and wearing fine garments.

Illuminated by the light from the ūrṇā-kośa between the Buddha’s eyebrows, it shone upon the seven-layered pavilion; looking eastward, I saw the Buddha standing outside the gate, his countenance as upright and serene as the moon among the stars, endowed with extraordinary marks and manifold excellences, his golden body composed and his faculties tranquil and settled.
The woman was filled with great joy and thought to herself:
"Now that I have been able to see the Buddha and his assembly of disciples, I shall resolve my mind to practice the conduct of a bodhisattva.
May I attain the Way just as the Buddha has!"
When Māra saw that the woman had conceived such a great resolve, his heart was filled with displeasure, and he thought to himself:
"This woman now generates great merit and seeks to become a Buddha; she will surely pass beyond my realm and deliver many people."
"Now I shall go and destroy his resolve for the Way.
Māra then descended and transformed himself into the appearance of a woman's father; dressed in her clothing, he said to Nāgadatta, "What you are currently contemplating is a very grave matter."
The Buddha-way is difficult to attain; only after diligent effort for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas without slackening does one finally achieve it.

Now that there is fortunately a Buddha in this world, it would be better to seek arhatship. Since it is easier to obtain and both lead to deliverance from the world, there is no difference between them regarding nirvāṇa.
"Why do you covet the Buddha and endure such long-term hardship?
You are my daughter; that is why I speak thus to you. Nāgadatta replied:
"It is not as your father said.
Although Arhats and Buddhas both transcend the world, their merits differ.
The Buddha’s wisdom is vast and encompassing, like the emptiness of the ten directions; his deliverance of beings is infinite."
"The wisdom of the Arhats is meager; it is as if they possess but a single ear.
Why would those of high talent delight in so little?
Māra spoke again:
"I have never heard that a woman can become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, much less become a Buddha!
The path of Buddhahood is long and arduous; it would be better to seek Arhatship and attain Nirvana early."
Nāgadatta replied,
"I have also heard that a woman cannot become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, cannot become Śakra, cannot become a Brahmā King, and cannot become a Buddha."
I shall apply myself with diligence so that, upon the completion of this female body, I may receive a male body.
For I have heard that those who practice the bodhisattva path throughout the world for hundreds of millions of kalpas without slackening will all eventually attain Buddhahood.
Seeing that the woman’s resolve would not waver, Māra became even more distressed and tormented; he further gave urgent instructions, saying:
"One who practices as a bodhisattva should not be greedy for the world, nor should they cherish their own life."
"Now, because you have exerted such diligence as to be able to throw yourself from the upper story to the ground, you shall later attain Buddhahood.
Nāgadatta thought to himself:
"Now that I have seen the Buddha, I truly desire the Bodhisattva path for myself."
"My father has taught that by casting off the body through diligence, one may attain the Way of the Buddha.
Why should I begrudge this fragile and precarious life?
The girl then joined her palms in reverence toward the Buddha from beside the railing and said:
"I now take refuge in the God among Gods; out of universal compassion, may You know my petition.
I pray that You spare my life and do not abandon the Bodhisattva, so that I may offer my body as a gift to the Buddha."
Having made this vow, she scattered flowers and cast herself down from the tower.
Before her body had even reached the ground, her female form was transformed into that of a man.
At that time, the Buddha smiled, and five-colored light issued from his mouth, illuminating an entire buddha-field before returning to enter through the crown of his head.
The Venerable Ānanda knelt before him and asked,
"The Buddha does not smile without cause."
"I wish to hear its meaning!
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!
"Do you see this woman who threw herself into the air and transformed into a man?
He replied, "I see her."
The Buddha said:

"This girl served ten thousand Buddhas in her previous lives and shall later make offerings to Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. After seventy-six million kalpas have passed, she shall attain Buddhahood, named Longsheng (Dragon Prosperity), with a lifespan of one kalpa."
After his parinirvāṇa, the Way of the Sūtras will flourish for half a kalpa before it finally ceases.
During that time, the Buddha will preach the Dharma, delivering nine billion seven hundred million people and causing them to attain the paths of Bodhisattvas and Arhats.
At that time, the food and drink of the people shall be like those in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Thereupon, Nāgadatta prostrated his body before the Buddha and addressed his parents, saying:
“I pray that you will release me, so that I may become a śramaṇa!”
The parents immediately granted their permission.
Five hundred kinsmen from various families and eight hundred devas, seeing that the woman Nāgadattā had been transformed into a man, all resolved to attain supreme, perfect enlightenment.
When the Mara King saw that the multitude were seeking the Buddha, his sorrow increased and he was no longer at ease; filled with shame, he returned home.
When the Buddha spoke these words, there was no one who did not rejoice.
The Sūtra on the Dragon-Girl Nāgadattā Spoken by the Buddha
